speechtext: "ROYAL anthem"

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the opening of the house yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in private conversation asked whether I would join with him in asking those present to sing the first verse of "God Save the Queen", as had been done last year. Naturally, I agreed wholeheartedly with the suggestion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext: Order. May I ask the Leader of the Opposition if he would raise this matter on the orders of the day.

subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext:
I am rising on a question of privilege, in view of the statement that I made a proposal of which I was unaware at the time. The Prime Minister used these words, as reported at page 4001 of Hansard:
Today the people of Canada are celebrating officially the anniversary of Her Majesty's birthday. In this house, as in other years, we will be evidencing our devotion to Her Majesty by continuing to give consideration to the public business of her Canadian subjects. But with your permission the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and I would like to suggest that before doing so we stand and sing together the first verse of the royal anthem.
I was not aware of the words that were to be used, and of course I do not suggest that there was any discussion of the actual words that would be used. I did not have an opportunity to mention this yesterday, because naturally the members all rose immediately and sang "God Save the Queen". In view of the fact that there is a tendency for statements placed on record to establish precedents, and that my name was joined in this suggestion, I do think it appropriate that I should ask the Prime Minister what was the significance of the words "royal anthem" used on this occasion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I assure the Leader of the Opposition that there was no other intention than to express our devotion to our beloved sovereign by singing the anthem which is a prayer for her success in this life and happiness in the hereafter. I had
given no previous thought to the way in which it could be described. It is the anthem which has been spontaneously accepted by the loyal subjects of Her Majesty and her predecessors throughout the commonwealth. I hope it offends no one to call it the royal anthem.
It seems to me it is significant that the loyal subjects of our sovereign throughout the commonwealth should wish to express in the form of a prayer their devotion to the beloved head of this great organization of which we are all the loyal subjects, and proud to be so.

subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question?

subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext:
This subject, I think, could more properly be raised on the orders of the day. The Leader of the Opposition had reason to raise it as a question of privilege because he had been associated with the suggestion yesterday and therefore I allowed him to state his point. If there are to be any further questions asked with respect to the exchange between the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition I think they should wait until we reach the orders of the day.

On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext:
In
connection with the question that was raised a moment ago by the Leader of the Opposition on a question of privilege, I should like to ask the Prime Minister, is it not a fact that "God Save the Queen" is our national anthem?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext:
"God Save the Queen" has never to my knowledge been adopted by any act of parliament or any resolution or any proclamation. It has by usage, I think, been spontaneously accepted by all the subjects of the British crown that they express their devotion to the crown in that form. I do not know any Canadian who is not glad to participate to the extent of his vocal powers in singing that hymn.
Whether it should be called a national anthem or whether it should be called a national prayer, I really do not know. I know it is honoured by all Canadians, and I know there are a good many Canadians who also

Inquiries of the Ministry like to pay similar honours to the other hymn, "O Canada". There have been debates in this house about national anthems and national flags. I do not think a debate over national anthems has ever been any cause of division. The debate over the national flag has caused expressions of very contradictory feelings, and I do not think Canada gains anything by controversies of that kind. I have always regarded both the tune and the words of "God Save the King" as an expression of devotion to the throne which is an essential part of our social organization, and I hope it will long remain a central part of it.
There have been suggestions that some of us on this side of the house objected to the word "royal". I think that is absolute nonsense. The hon. member and I expressed, I think, the feelings of practically all Canadians when we were considering the bill with respect to the royal style and titles. The hon. member recalls with what deep emotion and unanimity the sentiments we both expressed on that occasion were greeted by all our fellow members in the house. I hope that also will remain true.

subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext: May I direct a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. What is the national anthem of Canada? Is it "O Canada" or is it "God Save the Queen"? If the Prime Minister is not able to give a definite answer, is he as Prime Minister concerned about the matter, and is he prepared to bring in a recommendation to the house and to the people of Canada as to what is our national anthem?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to bring in any recommendation to the house to establish anything by law as a national anthem. I do not think that procedure has been necessary in any country of the commonwealth. The spontaneous feelings of the people of the commonwealth have always sufficed to indicate to them in what manner they could best express their devotion to the crown.

subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister answer my first question? Is there a national anthem for Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. DREW  SIGNIFICANCE OF USE OF WORDS
speechtext: I do not know of any legislative provision made in this house or in the parliament of any other of the nations of the commonwealth establishing by legislation that such or such is the national anthem.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
for leave to introduce Bill No. 410, to amend the Customs Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the essential purpose of this bill is to clarify and bring up to date certain sections of the Customs Act.
The present law only requires vehicles to report to customs when conveying dutiable goods. As the house is aware, my department is now charged with the administration of other regulations such as those involving the health of animals, insect infestations and diseases of plants, etc., and in addition the departments of immigration and health are concerned that everyone crossing the border should report.
An amendment is being proposed to the valuation sections which clarifies and confirms our present principles of valuation. It is also proposed to limit the period following the date of entry for appeals against original appraisal.
The tariff board will be empowered to hear appeals from departmental rulings affecting export drawback as well as domestic drawback. At the present time, if goods are diverted from use for which free entry or a lesser rate of duty was accorded, we can only make demand for the proper duty from the person found in possession. It seems desirable to also hold the original importer responsible in cases of this kind.
At the present time a lien holder has only 30 days from the date of seizure to apply for a judicial order to declare his interest in the goods or vehicle seized, and it is proposed to extend this time to 60 days. I shall be glad to give further details when the bill is up for second reading or when we get into committee.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, May 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Marler for the second reading of Bill No. 351, respecting Canadian National Railways, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Thatcher.

subtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to conclude what I said last evening, we must revert to fundamentals. Anyone will realize that there is a basic difference between the Canadian National Railways on the one hand and the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other company on the other hand. In the first place, Canadian National Railways are owned by the people of Canada whom we represent in the House of Commons, and all private companies are owned by their shareholders, who can decide about the management of their own companies by virtue of the companies acts of Canada and of the provinces. This distinction is essential, and it is the reason I have insisted so much on parliamentary control over the management of Canadian National Railways.
This Bill No. 351 is a great improvement because it contains many suggestions I have made, and especially those made on April 29. I do not take credit for their inclusion in the bill. I give the whole credit to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) and to the government. Since I am precluded, not because of the rules of the house but because of a practice which might be changed when the committee on rules reports, from mentioning the clauses of the bill I cannot refer to each one by number. However, I might say that if my colleagues take the trouble to read the bill they will realize that many important enactments are made concerning the bylaws governing the meetings of the board of directors and the qualifications of the directors of Canadian National Railways with regard to the subsidiary companies.
There is something new that I have not suggested. It is that officers and employees of the subsidiary companies can be appointed to the board of directors of such company. I am opposed to that. I cannot move now that the particular section be changed, but the members of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines may wish to take the matter into consideration when the bill comes before that committee. In my view it would be an error to appoint as directors, and so give the power of control to, any of those gentlemen who are in the management of any one of those subsidiary companies.


That being said, and since in each matter there is a part that is good and a part that is not so good and we have to weigh what is good and what is bad, I would say that in this case this bill is so much better than previous legislation I cannot do otherwise than vote against the six-months' hoist. I shall conclude by saying that the Canadian National Railways are a necessity in this country, because we must have railway competition. The Canadian taxpayer has made great sacrifices to promote the Canadian National Railways, and to give the railway the opportunity to serve the people of Canada at large we must take advantage of this new legislation. If it is not perfect now it is better than it was, and it could be made still better in due course. Therefore, sir, I shall vote against the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher).

subtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find myself completely at a loss to understand the furor of opposition by the Conservative party, the Social Credit party and the triumvirate independent party to the second reading of this bill. The Conservative party, the Social Credit party and the triumvirate independent party under the leadership of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) all believe completely in free enterprise.

subtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: Do you not?

subtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: No. They are completely sold on the idea that the best interests of Canada and the economy of Canada can be served by wide open competition; and yet, Mr. Speaker, it was most amazing to listen yesterday to speeches on this bill in which they expressed their opposition to such competition. In all their presentations they indicated that they did not want competition, unless of course it was only among companies owned privately. When it comes to competition between a privately owned company and a company owned by the taxpayers of Canada they do not want it.

subtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: That is not true at all.

subtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: Well, sir, if I may make my remarks I shall do so. If my hon. friend does not like them, I cannot help it.

subtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: I just want you to state the facts, that is all.

subtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
But his facts are not facts at all. Mr. Speaker, I am basing all my remarks on the introductory words of the Minister of Transport when he moved second reading of the bill and the comments made by the

Conservative members, and I include the Leader of the Opposition. I am very glad he is here today, because I intend to refer to his remarks and to the statements made by the members to my left, the Socreds, and the independents.
I have always understood that those who support private enterprise believe in competition. I have always understood that they believe in businesslike methods and efficiency; and if a company cannot stand competition, then it is a case of the devil take the hindmost. That is private enterprise as I understand it.
May I deal first of all with the purpose of this bill, which is what? I cannot understand anyone who believes in private enterprise, based on efficiency and businesslike methods -and especially when it comes from lawyers -opposing this bill. What have we before us? We have a bill which will consolidate in one act of parliament all the operations of the Canadian National Railways. As was pointed out by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton), who is a lawyer, now we have an operation that consists of 65 companies and 25 acts of parliament. On a basis of efficiency and businesslike operation, surely it is in the interests of all that 65 companies and 25 acts of parliament should be consolidated into one act. For the life of me I cannot understand any criticism when it is levelled at a desire to consolidate 65 companies and 25 acts into one act of parliament. To me that is common sense; to me that is efficiency. To my way of thinking it should meet with the acquiescence of everyone, businessmen and legal men alike.
I now want to come to the matter of private enterprise and competition. You know, sir, I was amazed at the speech made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition. I understand that he is called a brilliant leader of the opposition. I understand that he was-perhaps he is now-a very prominent member of the legal profession. Well, I will not challenge that, but I certainly cannot understand it because I never heard a more confused speech in my life than the one made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition when he spoke on the second reading of this bill. He wants competition and he believes in free enterprise. My interpretation of his remarks is that he believes in competition and free enterprise so long as there is no competition from a company owned by the taxpayers of Canada.
I want to quote from the remarks made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition, 50433-2561
Canadian National Railways recorded on page 4024 of Hansard. The remarks are to be found in the third paragraph of the second column, as follows:
Let us just see where this goes. If this right is given to the Canadian National Railways, is that an indication that the government is going to do the same kind of thing it does in regard to the C.B.C. and give to the government-chosen agency rights which deny fair competition as between, private enterprise and government agencies? If so. then it must confer the same right on the Canadian Pacific.
Then an hon. member interjected:
They have it.
I am admitting now that I was the member who said, "They have it".

My hon. friend asks, "Haven't they got that?" I am not going to spend time rereading what I read just now, but he should read it for himself. I cannot speak for the other provinces of Canada, but I can speak for British Columbia. The British Columbia electric railway operates in that province, and I have never heard of any Conservative or socred raising his hands in holy horror at the thought of the British Columbia railway taking over the Pacific stage lines which operate not only in British Columbia but on an international basis. They are operating now in Vancouver from the same ticket office and the same station.
I might mention the Canadian Pacific Railway. I cannot remember hearing of a Tory or socred raising his voice in horror in opposition to the C.P.R. owning the Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway on Vancouver island, which has taken over through a subsidiary both the passenger and trucking rights on Vancouver island through the purchase of the Vancouver Island Coach Lines and the Island Freight

Canadian National Railways lines. For years they have been operating that subsidiary, and I know that in Port Alberni the station and ticket office of the E. and N., which is owned by the C.P.R., is used by the coach lines and the freight lines of Vancouver island. To my knowledge that is the situation in British Columbia, in the case of this privately owned railway.
Why this opposition on the part of those who believe in equality and equity for private enterprise? Tories to my right and socreds to my left are going to deny to this company owned by the people of Canada the rights enjoyed by private shareholders, many of whom are not even residents of Canada.

What we want is that they
should not be given more rights than can be given under this bill.

We will come to that. I am
speaking from knowledge, and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) should know that as well. However, I notice that he did not speak on the bill or raise that point.

speechtext:
In his concluding remarks the Leader of the Opposition suggested that the bill should be held over until a dominion-provincial conference was called. I know what I am saying is correct because I am referring to his remarks as reported on page 4025 of Hansard of May 23. Here is what the Leader of the Opposition said:
I submit that before this bill is proceeded with there should be another conference with the provincial governments.
I can appreciate that statement, but I am puzzled to know what is the policy of the Conservative group in this house. First of all we have the Leader of the Opposition saying that before this bill is proceeded with there should be a conference with the provincial governments. I checked back on a statement made by another Conservative member of this house which received a great deal of editorial support. I refer to a speech made on May 10, 1955 by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) to be found on page 3647 of Hansard. The hon. member said:
I am suggesting that by dealing with dominion-provincial conferences the executive here, the cabinet, is not fulfilling its responsibilities to the House of Commons itself. This is a place where government programs should first be put forward, not at conferences.
What is the Conservative policy on this? In complete compliance with the wishes of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre the government have brought forward their program in the form of this bill, but then we are


told by the Leader of the Opposition that it should not be done by the cabinet, that the government should call a dominion-provincial conference.
We must realize that the railroads of Canada initially came into being because the taxpayers of Canada granted them rights. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre does not like this bill because it may cost the taxpayers some money. Many years ago the people of Canada gave the C.P.R. a subsidy of billions of dollars. They were given the right to everything contained in a strip 20 miles wide on each side of the railroad across the Dominion of Canada. On Vancouver island the E. and N., which they purchased, have been given the right to everything on the ground, above the ground and under the ground. The taxpayers of Canada have paid plenty.
The Canadian National Railways were taken over on what I consider was a wrong basis. We cannot do anything about that now, but instead of taking over the roads concerned on a bankrupt basis a capitalist Conservative government of Canada took them over in order to save private enterprise, and the taxpayers of Canada have been paying for it ever since.
Now we have this bill before us. I think the consolidation feature is right, because it brings into one act the operations of some 65 companies and 25 acts. This act, as I read it, is only asking that the Canadian National, owned by the people of Canada, shall now have the same rights as are being exercised by private railway companies in Canada. I cannot speak for all, but I do speak from my knowledge of the British Columbia Electric and the C.P.R. in their operations in British Columbia. Why cannot the C.N.R. have the same rights?
As I read this act the major thing for which they are asking is what the Conservatives and the socreds have always asked, that government operations shall be on an efficient and businesslike basis. If the Canadian National Railways find that it is inefficient and unprofitable to operate a line they ask for the right- which they have not had before, except as a subsidiary company-to be allowed to replace that passenger and freight transportation with passenger bus and truck lines so as to give service to the people who have been served by the railway itself.

That is not what the bill states, and you find it in a certain section. I do not believe the cabinet minister would stand up in this house and deliberately give a lie to the House of Commons. The minister stood in

He said the C.N.R. were in a difficult position because they wanted to be able to say that towns and municipalities would be served in some other way.
I cannot understand any supporters of free enterprise demanding by their opposition to this bill that the C.N.R. should operate on an inefficient basis. We have a request that they should be allowed to operate on an efficient basis. I also know something about dominion-provincial relations and, unless I am wrong, if it comes to a straight provincial operation on truck lines and passenger lines, they do come under provincial jurisdiction.

Here are the actual powers conferred on Canadian Pacific Transport Company Limited by the incorporating act under which they operate:
(a)	1. To carry on the business of transportation of passengers and goods of all kinds by land and water.
2.	To purchase, construct, hire, operate, maintain, repair, let, sell and dispose of conveyances, vehicles and vessels of all kinds drawn or propelled by any power whatever, including wagons, carts, trucks, carriages, automobiles, omnibuses, boats and aeroplanes.
3.	To carry on the business of forwarders, transportation agents, warehousemen and wharfingers and to construct, purchase, lease, hire, use and dispose of wharves, buildings, plant and appliances requisite for such purposes;
(b)	To purchase, rent, take, hold and enjoy lands, wharves, docks, warehouses, offices, elevators and other buildings in Canada or elsewhere to be used for the purposes of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or its steamship connections;
(c)	To enter into arrangements with a railway company or steamships company or other transportation company, and to obtain from such company any rights, privileges and concessions which the company may think it desirable to obtain, and to carry out, exercise and comply with any such arrangements, rights, privileges and concessions.
There are the powers conferred upon the Canadian Pacific Transport Company Limited. The hon. member for Vancouver East says, "But why not let Canadian National

Canadian National Railways Railways have the same powers?" He suggests they are just toeing given the same powers in section 27 of the bill now before us. If there was anything in that argument of course it might hold water, but it does not. Let us see what powers the Canadian National Railways have, quite irrespective of section 27 of the bill. These are the powers of Canadian National Transportation Limited under letters patent issued pursuant to the Companies Act, and are the powers under which they are carrying on business. Listen to the similarity to the Canadian Pacific powers. They are:
(a)	To carry on the business of transportation, for hire, of persons, goods, wares, merchandise, mails, property and things of every description, on land, water, and by air, or combinations thereof, by any means whatsoever, except by rail and except as a railway company;
(b)	To manufacture, buy, sell, hire, lease, import, export, operate and deal in vehicles, vessels, aircraft equipment, apparatus, engines, machines, mechanical contrivances or devices of every kind and description, using any form of motive power, which may be required, used or capable of being used in connection with any such business, and all machinery, accessories, parts, appliances, tools, supplies, materials and things required, used or capable of being used in connection therewith;
(c)	To interchange traffic with any railway company by container system or any method deemed desirable, and to furnish all necessary cars, trucks, equipment and apparatus, also to make agreements for the conduct and regulation of such traffic;
(d)	For the better carrying on of the business of the company to carry on the business of warehousemen, warfingers and storers of goods, wares and merchandise of every kind and description.
What could be covered in the way of transportation, Mr. Speaker, that is not covered by that? This is the company that carries on all business other than rail service. This company has full power to buy and sell motor vehicles, aircraft, ships and everything that can be used for transportation outside of railway vehicles themselves, which are covered by the general Railway Act. The situation is that Canadian National Transportation Limited, the subsidiary dealing with these types of transportation, has just as wide powers as the subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company engaged in the same field outside of rail activities. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, far from Canadian National Railways not having the powers the Canadian Pacific has, it has precisely the same powers under a federal act, and can carry on under that authority without having section 27 of this bill.
The thing every hon. member should ask- in this case the hon. member for Vancouver East, as well as other members-is why we are asked to pass section 27. Either section 27 means nothing or it means that some new powers are being conferred over and above


these wide powers I have just read in the act under which Canadian National Railways can buy and sell automobiles, aircraft and ships. Now, that is a very different authority than that which is conferred upon the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific may construct branches and extensions under authority granted by the board of transport commissioners. Under the new provision the Canadian National Railways is going to be allowed to do this by order in council. We know it is a loosening up process. You will recall the restriction that all contracts must be by tender, and provision that in certain cases, if the contract does not exceed $15,000, tenders need not be called. The Canadian National are not going to be called upon to go to the board of transport commissioners for approval if the branch line does not exceed six miles in length; they may get permission by order in council. There certainly can be no question that this party does not object in any way to a consolidation act. We think that is long past due and should be done; but we do object to a great many things that are in the bill before us.
Certainly we have never on any occasion objected to free competition. We have emphasized on many occasions that we think the railways, the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway, are entitled to compete with the trucking and other transport systems clear across this country. The only thing I have objected to on almost every occasion is the unfair competition that the railways are endeavouring to provide by legislation. It will not be competition; it will be an instrument to destroy their competitors.
We think it will be wrong from a national standpoint for the railways to have such powers over their competitors. They will not be competing with them; they will be strangling them so they will have a complete monopoly of all transportation in this country. That is the thing we object to. We have no objection to this bill in so far as it consolidates railway measures. We have objection to the exceptional powers that would be given to the railways, to the Canadian National Railways particularly, if this bill should go through in its present form.
It would not be necessary, as I indicated yesterday, for the railways to put into effect the agreed charges contracts they now have the legal right to enter into, and that is a very potent weapon in strangling the competition from trucks. Under this legislation they could go much further than that. They could violate all provincial legislation if this legislation is enacted in its present form.

Of course they did then, but this bill was not law at that time. If this bill goes through, under clause 27 and clause 18 the railways will not have to ask permission from the provinces. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in dealing with the matter of public transportation I do not believe the people of Canada are too much concerned about the straw man of provincial rights which has been raised in this house. I endorse what was said yesterday by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) when he contended that this problem of public transportation must be viewed as a whole, and that we must evolve a plan which will give the public transportation at as low a rate as possible. I think this provincial rights issue is simply a bogeyman that has been introduced.
I was a little surprised that the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre should introduce this amendment with the argument which he put forth. If the Canadian National Railways are losing money each year I would imagine, in the light of his attitude in past years, that he would be the last one to oppose any move that would enable the Canadian National Railways to put itself in a position where it could avoid heavy deficits each year. I have every sympathy for the taxpayers of Canada and would like to help them all I can, and I therefore think the Canadian National Railways should be given every assistance in reducing these deficits.
I submit that one of the reasons for the annual deficits of the Canadian National Railways can be traced directly to the Conservative party. I notice that they take every credit for having initiated the Canadian National railway system, but when that was done they did not consider the welfare of the people of Canada. When this system was set up first consideration was given to the welfare of the bondholders of what should have become bankrupt railroads. There have been no more able spokesmen for the C.P.R. in this house than the members of the Conservative party. I notice that the new Conservatives, the socreds, are most anxious to climb on the bandwagon and take up cudgels on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. One would almost

imagine that the Canadian Pacific was going to offer a full slate of candidates of its own at the next federal election.
To speak of free competition in the matter of public transportation is about as unrealistic as to advocate free competition in the distribution of public services such as hydroelectric power. The Canadian National Railways belongs to the people of Canada. Accusations are being made in this house by independents, the Social Credit and the Conservative parties, in connection with certain rights being granted to the Canadian National Railways which they contend would not be good for the people of Canada.
We must remember that the Canadian National Railways must appear annually before the members of the House of Commons. If there is misuse of the powers that have been granted I shall be ready, along with other members of parliament, to attack the minister and the Canadian National Railways for such misuse of power. I say again that if we are honestly concerned over the welfare of the taxpayers of Canada we will do everything possible to enable this railway system to so operate that it can provide transportation for people and goods at the lowest possible cost, and perhaps be able to rid the taxpayers of this annual deficit. We shall examine their operations once a year in democratic fashion, as we have done in years gone by.

The real question was not about shareholders but whether the creditors could be paid.
We must remember that since that time the government has forgiven hundreds of millions of dollars of debt due to it. The shareholders so far have been out of the picture, and we really should not bring them in as if in some way they had been badly treated. They have disappeared from the picture, except perhaps in one or two small lines where the shareholders may have got something. I appreciate the dilemma in which our friends at the south end of the chamber find themselves with regard to a package bill. The hon. member for Bow River indicates that there are things in this bill that he wants; but he must vote for the amendment, which is the six months' hoist, because of his opposition to one or two features of the bill which he does not like. We are all in that position at times. On that basis, Mr. Speaker, it seems to us in this group that on balance this legislation should in principle be supported and sent to the committee. In the main it is a consolidation of the many statutes with regard to the Canadian National Railways, and it will make possible a more efficient and more effective administration of that system on behalf of the people of Canada.
I must confess, even if there are one or two minor points about which there is some question, that I am surprised that there should be any number of members of this house who want to do what they can to prevent this bill from being supported in principle, which is the effect of the six months' hoist. I shall not mind that being quoted against us on occasions when we move the six months' hoist to legislation with which we disagree.
Like the Leader of the Opposition, I feel a number of things have been done by the management of the Canadian National Railways which I do not like. I did not like the

Canadian National Railways Pitt affair in Winnipeg, not at all. I still do not like the way in which the Canadian National Railways board of directors sold two Canadian National hotels and two summer resorts. I do not like what has been done with respect to the Queen Elizabeth hotel in Montreal, in that it is being let out for management purposes to the Hilton chain in the United States. I certainly do not like the way employees have been laid off by the Canadian National Railways during the past several months. I had something to say about that yesterday when I read a letter to the House of Commons. Likewise I am bitterly disappointed that it has taken so long for the Canadian National Railways to reconsider the position of their pensioners, particularly those in the lower brackets and, if I may go one step further, I say particularly those whose only pension is $25 a month.
I hope some of these matters will be given more serious consideration than has yet been the case. But, even after one has registered all the complaints he has against the management of the Canadian National Railways, it is still a fact that we want the Canadian National Railways to have a decent and proper charter, which is the purpose of this legislation. For that reason it seems to us that this bill should receive approval by being given second reading, and if one takes that position one must oppose the six months' hoist which is now before the house.
So far as the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Bow River are concerned, far be it from me to defend the Minister of Transport, as too many things he does call for attack as far as I am concerned; but he made a statement yesterday which cut the ground from under a good deal of what has been said by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Bow River. He admitted that some change might have to be made so it would be clear that a certain section of the bill did not make all the companies mentioned in a certain schedule works for the general advantage of Canada. He specifically referred to Canadian National Transportation Limited.
The Leader of the Opposition today listed the powers Canadian National Transportation now has, and they seem to be even greater than those that are suggested in the relevant part of the bill. It strikes me that all that is sought is a consolidation of the powers and rights that now obtain so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned. If our friends to the right and our friends to the left and those to the far left-geographically, not politically, of course-favour consolidation, they should support the bill rather than the six months' hoist.

The Leader of the Opposition has dealt with those provisions in detail, and I do not intend to cover the ground covered by him. Certainly the arguments he advanced have not been met, and it seems clear to me that one or two sections in this bill are deliberately designed to take the government out of the quagmire in which it placed itself last year when it tried to play both ends against the middle.
First it went to the privy council, it went to the courts, in order to uphold the right of the federal government to control motor transportation. Then, having succeeded, it came to the conclusion that it could not discharge its responsibilities and had an act passed by parliament to remove it from the difficulties in which it found itself. Now again, under the subterfuge of consolidation, it is endeavouring to restore to itself the powers which the provinces had the right to expect under the agreement made at the conference and also under the statute passed at the last session of parliament.
Indeed, in looking over the act I find that seven of the 47 clauses are new and in no way consolidations. In addition to that, there are two major subsections that are completely new. Why dispose of them at all, my hon. friend says. I repeat that, but apparently repetition of actual facts and desirable conclusions is looked upon with a certain amount of suspicion. I repeat what I have said. The bill in its present form is merely a means whereby the government, having agreed to measures that on the face of them gave every appearance of a sincere desire to preserve and protect provincial rights, is seeking by the back door method to bring in a section which, as it now stands, will permit Canadian National Railways to override provincial authority and give them a field of authority above that conferred upon the provinces last year by an act of this parliament passed in June of 1954.
Sir, what is needed today is not a consolidation of statutes, although that is helpful. What is needed is an attitude of mind upon the part of those in authority on the Canadian National Railways that will bring about a restoration of morale among the railway employees and give them that impetus and desire to assist they had at one time but which has been torn from them by the attitude of those in charge of Canadian National Railways within the last several years. As far as the consolidation is concerned, there will be no argument about it whatsoever, but I ask the minister to say when he replies why, under the guise of consolidation, he brings in by a back door method sections which designedly contravene everything declared as

an abiding principle one year ago and which will not have the effect of improving the administration of Canadian National Railways but will have the effect of undoing that which was done with such expressions of sanctity last year when a bill was brought before the house and ultimately translated into legislation.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) made the statement that we have a committee of parliament which will permit us to examine. That does not meet the situation at all. As far as the minister is concerned, let me say to him that it has been more difficult for parliament to get information expeditiously than it was in the past. Assurance has already been given that the bill will go before a standing committee of the house, but parliament has a right to ask on this occasion that there will be some realization on the part of Canadian National Railways and those in charge of its operations of what the little man on the railway says today. For some reason the encouragement he should be receiving is not being provided, and the opportunity to expand and develop the business is being denied him by methods which he believes to be detrimental to the company that he honours and that we honour. I am opposed to the six months' hoist and I say that so far as the sections having to do with consolidation are concerned they necessarily should be accepted. But after the bill has been considered by the committee and the minister has given further consideration to the sections that in our opinion are and will be detrimental to the operation of the railway an opportunity will arise on third reading to ascertain what is the will of the majority in the House of Commons.

Canadian National Railways if a member is repeating until you have heard him, and once you have heard him he has completed his repetition and therefore you cannot ask him to swallow his words. Therefore the only thing the Speaker can do is to ask hon. members for their co-operation, and that is what I was doing with respect to the hon. member for Prince Albert.
Whenever a debate lasts a certain length of time, it is almost inevitable that in the latter stage of the debate these repetitious arguments will occur. speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, May 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Weaver for the second reading of Bill No. 376, to authorize Trans-Prairie Pipelines, Ltd., to construct, own and operate an extra-provincial pipe line.

subtopic: TRANS-PRAIRIE PIPELINES, LTD.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a somewhat different pipe line bill from the ones we have been accustomed to in recent years. According to the explanatory note:
The purpose of this bill is to authorize TransPrairie Pipelines, Ltd., a company incorporated under the laws of the province of Manitoba, to construct, own and operate an extra-provincial pipe line or pipe lines.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, when one starts to speak on one of these private pipe line bills one misses the former member for Fraser Valley who always took an active part in these discussions.
This bill is entirely different in its structure from the pipe lines that we have been considering since the passage of the general Pipe Lines Act. I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) pointed that out very clearly last Friday when he spoke on this bill. The bills that have come before us as private pipe line bills were in effect bills granting charters to incorporate companies. In those Gills was a long list of provisions similar to the provisions contained in practically all of the private pipe line bills we have discussed since the introduction of the general Pipe Lines Act. We in this group view this bill with certain suspicions although things may turn out better than we expect. This bill simply authorizes a company chartered under the laws of Manitoba to enter into the pipe line business. There are no further details as to the area it intends to serve, who will be the directors, what will be the capital or as to the many other provisions which are spelled out in other pipe line bills we have discussed.
We are very interested in knowing why there should be this short form of bill. The other bills which came before this house were to some extent the result of lengthy debates in the house by members of all parties, particularly those on this side, who were anxious to protect Canadian interests in the development of natural resources and to see that Canadian requirements, particularly with

respect to the distribution of gas and oil, were met prior to the requirements of anyone outside the country.
The other companies were aware of the discussion that had taken place, they were aware of government policy with respect to the building of pipe lines for the distribution of gas and oil, and were willing to comply with the established procedure in order to have their bills come before this house in a form following the common practice. They were willing to come before the committee and state what they had in mind, what their intended developments would cover, and on several occasions when requested by members of the committee, particularly the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), who has been most active in this type of debate, they agreed to amendments to their bills in order to meet specific objections by opposition members, and on some occasions by members on the government side.
We cannot understand the reason for this short-cut type of bill. We are afraid it may be the commencement of a breakdown of the practice which has been established during recent years in connection with private pipe line bills. We have only the bill in front of us on which to form an opinion, but in our view it can mean several things if adopted in its present form. It certainly would appear to provide for very little control over the development and building of pipe lines. Second, it could mean the breakdown in protection for the public which has been built up after considerable effort both inside and outside the house. Third, it could possibly destroy the opportunity for the parliament of Canada to satisfactorily develop a national policy with respect to the development and distribution of gas, oil and petroleum products.
For these reasons we in this group feel we shall have to oppose second reading. We feel the bill is unsound in principle, in form and structure. We feel we must do this unless the sponsor can assure the house that this company will be agreeable to amendments being introduced in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines which will meet the objections raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and this group and thus place this bill on a par with other private pipe line bills that have come before this house. If the sponsor of the bill can assure the house that these objections will be met in full then I think this group can support the motion for second reading.

SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, May 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles for the second reading of Bill No. 379, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege of making part of my speech on the second reading of this bill on Friday, May 20. At that time I dealt mainly with history and made reference to certain sessional papers which had been tabled in days gone by, in response to questions I had asked showing my longstanding interest in the question as to whether or not cabinet ministers should be at the same time directors of private companies. I also invited hon. members to read the very interesting debates on this question which took place in the House of Commons in 1921


and 1922. I made reference to these debates of 1921 and 1922 both for their own sake and to support my contention that this matter is not one that has arisen in the public mind only recently but rather one that has been the concern of members of parliament and the concern of public men for a good many years.
I indicated at the close of my remarks on Friday that I would make reference today to certain practices connected with this subject matter. I must say quite readily that I have not been able to ascertain that any country where the situation is similar to ours has legislation of the kind proposed in my bill, making it a statutory provision that ministers not hold directorships in private companies. Particularly I must say that there is, as far as I can ascertain, no such legislation in the United Kingdom or in the United States. However, hon. members are aware of the practice in the United Kingdom which in more recent years in particular has been quite definite in that, as a matter of routine and as a matter of practice, ministers do not hold directorships in private companies. They exercise a very scrupulous practice in relation to private legislation that comes before the parliament at Westminster. Then, too, all of us are aware of what happened recently in the United States in the case of Mr. Charles Wilson, who found it necessary because of public opinion to divest himself, not only of any authority he exercised by way of directorship, but also of his holdings in a very large corporation in that country, before taking a post in President Eisenhower's cabinet.
I cite these examples freely admitting that they show that there is no legislation along this line, but also showing that there is a very strong feeling in countries like ours that cabinet ministers should not be directors of private companies.
I should like to say a word about the practice in our own country, particularly with reference to the most important member of the cabinet. I am not referring only to the present situation, but to the situation across the years. As I understand it, previous to Sir Wilfrid Laurier there were prime ministers who held directorships in small firms, but Sir Wilfrid Laurier gave up all but one small, shall we say, family directorship. In the case of the prime ministers we have had in Canada since that time, they have divested themselves of any and all directorships they might have held. That was the case with Sir Robert Borden; it was the case with the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen; and it was the

case with the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. I understand that the late Lord Bennett-he was Mr. Bennett at the time- gave up his directorships at the time he became the leader of the Conservative party in 1927. In the case of the present Prime Minister, as can be seen by reference to sessional paper No. 160-B, tabled on February 11, 1948, in response to questions of mine, he was sworn of the privy council on 10th of December, 1941, and five days later resigned all of his directorships. The sessional paper to which I have referred lists those 11 directorships which he resigned immediately after becoming a member of the cabinet. Of course, that was a long time before he became prime minister, but subsequent sessional papers have indicated that the present Prime Minister does not hold any directorships.
In other words, so far as the prime ministers of Canada are concerned, it is an accepted practice that in their view they should not be directors of private companies while they hold that very high office. Now, in view of my admission that I have not been able to find legislation comparable to my bill, the question arises-and it is a fair one-why ask for legislation; why not leave it, as the Prime Minister suggested, to the conscience of each individual cabinet minister?
First of all I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that things have changed a good deal since the early days when the Senate and House of Commons Act was first put into effect and when it was felt that the only kind of relationships that could exist between the people and the government in a business sense were in the terms of contracts or small offices that might involve emoluments. Things have changed considerably, particularly in this day when the government is involved in so many things in our economy and particularly in view of the change in respect of income tax and succession duty legislation. There are all kinds of ways today in which there is contact between private corporations and the government which were not the case in the earlier days of this country. I submit that on that score this whole question should be reassessed.
I have read a great many times, as other hon. members have done, and with a great deal of interest, the independence of parliament provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act. As hon. members know, squarely in the middle of the Senate and House of Commons Act there are ten or a dozen sections which make it a matter of statute that no member of parliament is to hold, while he is a member of parliament, any job under the crown to which any emolument is attached, no matter how small that
Senate and House of Commons Act job or that emolument might be. It is also made statutory that no member of parliament may have any contract with the government. No member of parliament may sell anything to the federal government, nothing whatsoever.
Mr. Speaker, as strongly as I can I make the point, that matter is not left to conscience. It is not left to my conscience or to the conscience of any other individual member whether we should try to get some little job under the government while we are members of parliament or whether we should try to get some contract with the government. It is laid down by statute that these things shall not be done.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in the case of cabinet ministers the situation is even more important and more crucial. If it is not left to the conscience of individual members of parliament whether or not they do things that might compromise the independence of parliament, I submit that it should not be left to the individual consciences of cabinet ministers. I suggest that there should be regulation there as well. I suggest there should be a statutory provision so that it will be crystal clear that no cabinet minister can have any other duty or obligation which can conflict in any way with his full-time responsibilities to the Canadian people as a cabinet minister.
As I say, I have read with considerable interest the independence of parliament provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act. I have also examined with some interest what the attitude of parliament has been across the years towards these provisions. Hon. members may know these facts but even if they do, they will not mind my recalling them to them.
There was an occasion when no less a person than the Speaker of the House of Commons was obliged to resign his seat in the House of Commons and to resign his speakership at the same time because he violated one of the independence of parliament sections. He happened to be the first Speaker under a Liberal regime. I hasten to add that in the examples I shall give in a moment I shall be quite fair; I shall name instances where both Liberals and Conservatives ran afoul of that particular law. In this case it was Mr. Speaker Anglin who represented a constituency in New Brunswick and who edited or owned a newspaper down in Saint John. I believe the name of it was the Freeman. It turned out that that paper carried some federal government notices or paid advertisements, and the committee on privileges and elections felt that procedure was a violation of the independence
4070	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons Act of parliament provisions in the Senate and House of Commons Act. As a result, Mr. Speaker Anglin was obliged to resign. Some time after the session of 1877 he ran in a by-election, was re-elected and came back to the House of Commons and was again elected to the Speaker's chair.
I may say that the late Mr. Anglin's re-election as Speaker in 1878 was not without an extremely acrimonious debate. I invite hon. members who are interested in our past as a parliament to read particularly the real "knock-'em-down and drag-'em-out" oratorical battle that took place between Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, who was then Liberal prime minister, and Sir John A. Macdonald, the leader of the Conservative opposition. Sir John objected strenuously to Mr. Anglin's even being seated back on the floor of the House of Commons before a Speaker had been elected, let alone his being elected as Speaker of the House of Commons. There may have been other occasions, but certainly on that occasion the result of that debate was that there was a recorded division as to whether or not Mr. Anglin should take the chair in 1878 as Speaker of the House of Commons. All of that fight and all of that furore was over the incident to which I have referred, namely the appearance in the Saint John Freeman of certain notices or advertisements inserted there by the federal government. The insertion of those notices was regarded as a violation of the independence of parliament provisions.
Let me come on down the years a bit, Mr. Speaker, and remind the house that in 1932 there was a Mr. Jones in the House of Commons. That was not my present colleague of course. This was Hon. George B. Jones who was the then Conservative member for Royal. He turned out to be the principal partner in the firm of Jones Brothers which had sold certain merchandise to the Indians, who were wards of the federal government. As a result of investigation in that case Mr. Jones resigned, although he too was re-elected. Similarly in the early part of this century there was the case of the then Liberal member for Glengarry, Mr. J. T. Schell, who, it was found, sold crates worth $5.50 to the dominion government. The matter was referred to the committee on privileges and elections. In his case he was able to satisfy that committee that this had been done without his knowledge, and he was not called upon to resign.
From their knowledge of history probably hon. members are more familiar with certain events that took place in 1915, during world war I. At that time certain matters were


referred to the committee on public accounts. As a result, two Conservative members of parliament-Mr. Foster from Kings, in Nova Scotia, and Mr. Garland who represented the constituency of Carleton-were obliged to resign. Mr. Foster was involved in some war contracts rather directly. In the case of Mr. Garland, it appears that he was one of the proprietors of a drug store here in Ottawa; and the record indicates that it was a boy working in his store who made to the federal government certain sales out of which he made a considerable profit. Mr. Garland was held responsible for this action.
If I may say so, to put it in language that will be understood, when I read in the Hansard of 1915 the things that Sir Robert Borden said about Mr. Garland and Mr. Foster, both of whom were his own members, I was reminded of what the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said when the case of Mr. Dewar, the former member for Qu'Appelle, arose in this house a few years ago. In other words, on all of these former occasions as well as in the case of the former member for Qu'Appelle-perhaps that case is a little bit different, although it included an involvement of a kind with a contractor who had relations with the government-in all these cases the house took an extremely serious view of the situation, and in all cases where the prime minister came into the picture, right across the years as leader of the house, whoever he was, Liberal or Conservative, he took an extremely serious view of any of these steps that seemed to involve a violation of the provisions of the independence of parliament sections of the Senate and House of Commons Act.
If we as a House of Commons have taken such a serious view of these things which, when we look at them, seem to be rather minor, should we not take an equally serious view of what I am concerned about in this bill that I present to parliament, namely the matter of cabinet ministers being directors of private companies.
When I began my remarks on Friday I said-and I ask the Prime Minister and others to remember it-that I raised this matter as one of principle. I do not raise it for the purpose of making an attack on a particular cabinet minister. Nevertheless I am going to mention something in relation to a particular cabinet minister because his case is, I think, a rather scandalous example of a bad practice. But I must say to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that the person whom I hold responsible, the person whom I think the house has to hold responsible for the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) continuing as a director of the

Guaranty Trust Company of Canada is the Prime Minister who said very clearly in the house the other day that he felt the matter should be left to the conscience of each individual cabinet minister. That is what I think is wrong. It is that as a principle which I am attacking.
I ask hon. members to listen to one or two sentences I want to read from the annual report of the Guaranty Trust Company of Canada for the year 1954. Incidentally, there is no question about it, on page 2 of the report the Minister of National Revenue- and that title is given to him in the report- is listed as one of the directors of the company. In this same annual report there are of course a number of propaganda or advertising paragraphs urging people to do business with the company. One of the paragraphs is entitled, "Administration of Estates", and reads in part as follows:
Guaranty Trust Company of Canada makes an ideal executor or administrator of an estate.
I skip a few sentences, and then I read this:
Each estate is in charge of a senior trust officer, supported by the advice and guidance of the executive officers, directors and local advisory boards . . .
Imagine, Mr. Speaker, once upon a time a Speaker of the House of Commons had to resign because some government notices appeared in a paper that he owned in Saint John, New Brunswick, but today the Prime Minister says it is all a matter of conscience when he has a colleague who is a director of a company which is administering estates, a director who, according to that company's advertising, gives his guidance and advice to that company's clients in such matters as succession duties. Yet, the same person sits on the other side of the table as Minister of National Revenue levying those succession duties. How can one be on both sides of the table at the same time?
I said a moment ago that I mention this only because it strikes me that it is a scandalous example of a bad practice, but the person I think we all must hold responsible for the continuation of this practice is the Prime Minister who, as he will readily admit, has taken the responsibility for laying down the principle that these things should be left to the conscience of individual cabinet ministers. I think that day has gone. I think the time has come when, if it is not left to our consciences as individual members of parliament whether we maintain the independence of parliament required by the Senate and House of Commons Act, the same statutory provision should be there so far as cabinet ministers are concerned.
Senate and House of Commons Act
As I say, I present this as a matter of principle. I present it as something that for my part has been a matter of long-standing interest. I present it as something that has been the concern of parliament right across the years. I hope very serious consideration will be given to it. I do not know what is going to happen to my bill. I know what happens to most bills that are introduced from the opposition side of the house. They do not get along very well the first time, but still it is true that across the years good ideas introduced on the opposition side of the house do have their way of being accepted in one way or another, and I hope that the principle I am presenting to the house in this bill will sooner or later be accepted, and sooner rather than later.
As for the Liberals, they of course can vote either way so far as precedent is concerned. I pointed out the other day that in 1921 most of the Liberals voted for a bill having the same effect as mine would have but in 1922 practically all the Liberals voted against a resolution to the same effect. In the case of the Conservatives, back in 1921 and 1922 most if not all of them voted against any statutory provision of this kind. Nevertheless I think that the Conservatives would do well to read what Arthur Meighen said on those occasions. In fact he was almost prophetic at one point where he said that the time might come when something along this line would have to be done. I have not checked with Arthur Meighen to find out, though he could be seen by those who are close to him, but my suspicion is that he who in 1921 and 1922 did not want this kind of legislation but wanted it crystal clear that no cabinet ministers should hold directorships, might say that if after all these years this kind of thing is still going on, the kind of thing to which I have alluded by reference to the annual report of the Guaranty Trust Company of Canada, it would appear that there is no solution to it but to bring in legislation to make it clear that being a cabinet minister is a full-time job.
I will be quite happy if the Prime Minister will make the kind of announcement that will make this legislation completely unnecessary. I do not need to spell out what the terms of that announcement would be. Perchance as he thinks the matter over he will agree with me that, rather than leaving it to the individual consciences of cabinet ministers and rather than leaving it as a responsibility resting upon the conscience of the Prime Minister alone, it might be better to have parliament make the decision. In any event, Mr. Speaker, I think we would be true to the best traditions of parliament, and we would be true to the concern of those who have

Senate and House of Commons Act gone before us in this place right back to 1867 if we would give very serious consideration to what is involved in the principle of the bill.
As I pointed out, long ago it was felt that any individual private member who did anything to compromise the independence of parliament should resign his seat, and that course has been followed on a number of occasions. I suggest that the position of cabinet ministers is even more important, and I hope that very serious consideration will be given by the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the cabinet and by all members of the Liberal party, the Conservative party and the other parties in the house to what I suggest is a very important proposition.
