The house resumed at eight o'clock. CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Marler for the second reading of Bill No. 351, respecting Canadian National Railways.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group support this measure not only because it is necessary for the operation of our nationally owned railway and because it is a tidying up of existing legislation, but also because it gives to the Canadian National Railways, as I understand it, the right to compete with the Canadian Pacific Railway on an equal basis. Certainly, if we are to expect from our nationally owned system a railway that will compete successfully with the privately owned system, we should be prepared to give it all the powers that the Canadian Pacific Railway now is able to exert in the transportation field.
We in this group particularly expect from our nationally owned railway system not only service as efficient as that from the privately owned railway but in fact a better service, a service that meets the needs of the Canadian people more adequately than that given by the privately owned railway.
In its operations the Canadian National Railways should, as I hope they do, look at the general economic well-being of the nation, and should not be governed solely by economy considerations. I am sure the Canadian National Railways do not like to show a large deficit year after year; but I believe more important than whether or not the Canadian National Railways may show a deficit is the kind of service that they may be able to provide to Canadians generally. Certainly, I believe that adequate service to the Canadian nation by the C.N.R. is more important at any given time than a C.N.R.

Canadian National Railways balanced budget. Since the Canadian National Railways is a nationally owned system, it might be cautious in laying off large numbers of employees, because by doing so it merely adds to the general employment difficulties of the nation. When the government is responsible, as it is, for full employment, we would not want the railroads doing anything that would unduly add to that responsibility.
We naturally understand the position of the C.N.R. in wishing to modernize its railway and to economize to the greatest possible extent. But I cannot help having full sympathy for those who find themselves displaced, and particularly the case mentioned the other day by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). In the main we look to the nationally owned railway system for the provision of service. I for one do not like to see any large and substantial whittling down of that service in an attempt to balance the budget of the C.N.R. I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) grinning. I do not think it is any worse for the C.N.R. to have an unbalanced budget than it is for the whole Canadian nation to have a nationally unbalanced budget as we have this year. Either one may be more in the interests of the nation at any given time than a precisely balanced budget.
Members of parliament, certainly those from the prairie areas, are having brought to their attention, more frequently in recent weeks and months, instances of a severe curtailment of railway service. My information may or may not be correct; but I have been informed that while the prairie area has been one of the main areas in which some services have been reduced, yet the main objective for reduction of services could shift from that area to another area.
I have said that we all like to see a balanced budget, yet I cannot help but sympathize with the people in those areas who suffer a cancellation of services or a reduction of services. I have obtained from the board of transport commissioners the record of reduction of train services and the closing of stations, at least as far as maintaining a station agent is concerned, since January 1, 1953. I find that in the province of Saskatchewan alone in 1953 there was a reduction affecting 19 trains and 9 lines in that province. The next year there was a reduction of service by only two trains on one line. In this year to date there has been a reduction of train service on 7 railway lines. This means that in the period from January 1, 1953, to the present there has been a reduction in service on 17 lines. This compares with a reduction of service in the same period on 5 Canadian Pacific Railway lines. There may

be reasons to explain the much larger number of C.N.R. lines that have had train service reduced, but certainly we expect from our C.N.R. as few reductions in our train service as possible.
I hold in my hand a table entitled "Removal of Station Agents in Saskatchewan granted since January 1, 1953". It says that on the C.N.R. in 1953 station agents at 3 points were removed; in 1954 station agents at 11 points were removed; and in 1955 to date station agents at 3 points have been removed. I believe in every case a caretaker has been substituted for the services of the station agent. But, as the minister knows a caretaker does not accept C.O.D. orders, and of course he is not able to transmit telegrams, and in fact can only give to the people in that community a very limited service compared with the service given by a station agent.
I have had brought to my attention a further unwarranted reduction in train service that is being contemplated by the C.N.R., namely, a proposed reduction in its present daily passenger service between the city of Weyburn and the city of Regina. This follows a cancellation of the passenger train service between the city of Weyburn and the town of Radville in 1953. The people in that area are very concerned about the reduction in train service. The mayor of the city, Mr. J. H. Stav-ely and the chairman of the chamber of commerce, Mr. D. Mann, have met with railway officials and have placed before them the position of the people in the area around the city of Weyburn and in the Radville district.
As I have said, we can quite understand the C.N.R. wishing to save as much as possible through cutting down railway services; but surely there is more to be considered than merely balancing the budget. It is true that the C.N.R. has applied for a trucking franchise along the Regina-Weyburn route in order to substitute a trucking service for the reduced services as far as freight and express are concerned. Communications I have had oppose this move. In fact it would be an unnecessary duplication of service.
Since as a nation we must maintain our railways, to the extent that freight traffic is removed from the railways by the railways themselves and placed in a trucking seivice, we the people of Canada are paying for two types of service. It is true also that as a nation, or as a province, we have to maintain our highways. Therefore, it is in the national interest that in so far as possible a national transportation policy should be adopted that

will permit our railways to provide the very best service and protect the general interests of the Canadian public.
Until we have a national transportation policy we are going to have more and more uneconomical competition between our trucking and railway lines. Trucking services, altogether apart from those operated by the railways in direct competition with the railways, will take away from them much of their traffic and the nation as a whole must maintain the rail services and therefore must pay for the maintenance of the railway right of way and at least reduced railway services. The nation as a whole must pay for the highway services and maintain the highways.
I am hopeful that the government will adopt a national transportation policy which will prevent further curtailment of the services that the railroads have provided and not make it necessary for the Canadian public to bear the cost of the duplication of services.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest and I think considerable attention to what has been said by the various hon. members who have participated in the debate on this bill. I think without exception all hon. members who have participated in the debate approve of the principle of the consolidation of what I might call the Canadian National legislation. However, one or two members have said that under the guise of consolidation or under the subterfuge of consolidation other things were being done in the legislation now before the house.
I do not think that those terms aptly describe what has been done because when I look back on the proceedings in connection with this legislation I find that the principal changes to be made were set forth in the resolution itself which made it perfectly clear that the purpose of the legislation was not only to consolidate the existing legislation but to make five particular changes. When I made a statement at the resolution stage of the bill I drew that to the attention of the house. Likewise when I made a statement on the second reading I endeavoured to point out the five changes which this legislation would bring about so far as Canadian National Railways was concerned.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) taxed me with a lack of frankness with regard to this measure and I want to say right away that I plead not guilty to that accusation. I think I have made it perfectly clear that no attempt is being made by calling this measure a consolidation to embody in it additional legislation of which the house has not had the fullest notice. During the course of my remarks at the resolution and 50433-257i
Canadian National Railways second reading stages I made it quite clear what purposes the government had in mind in bringing forward this legislation at this time. I should like to deal particularly with the powers which it is proposed to give to the railway company in the matter of what I might term highway transportation. In that connection I said yesterday, as reported on page 4021 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian National Railways, through its company, Canadian National Transportation, Limited, has very comprehensive highway powers; but it is not intended to give such comprehensive powers to the Canadian National Railways. As will be found by reference to the bill, it is intended only that the parent company shall have powers in conjunction with or substitution for a rail service.
In order to particularize the type of transportation services to which the bill was intended to apply, I then went on to say:
This is designed primarily in order to regularize the pickup and delivery services in the metropolitan centres, and to give the company corporate powers to enable it to provide trucking or bus services in cases in which rail line abandonment would not be permitted by the board of transport commissioners, unless a formal undertaking with regard to road transport were submitted.
During the debate at the resolution stage when dealing with services in substitution for rail services I explained the position of the railway company very fully. I do not think I have anything either to add to or subtract from the two statements to which I have just referred. I think they set forth fully and frankly the exact powers that we wish to give to the Canadian National Railways.
If it had been the sinister purpose of the government to enable the Canadian National Railways to exercise the extensive powers it has through its subsidiary companies I believe it would have been possible to have made use of the legislation to which the Leader of the Opposition referred yesterday and this afternoon, the Motor Vehicle Transport Act which was passed last year. This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition read to the house the extensive powers of Canadian National Transportation, Limited, and I was glad that I had said yesterday that it was not our intention to declare that these works should be for the general advantage qf Canada. There is no intention whatever on the part of the government to broaden the already broad powers which the subsidiary company possesses and to which the Leader of the Opposition referred this afternoon.
I should like to emphasize that the reason we wish to give these powers to the railway company is that they are in fact exercised by the railway company and not by the subsidiary. Pickup and delivery services of the

Canadian National Railways railway company are carried out by the railway company itself and not by the subsidiary in the principal metropolitan centres. I understand that that is not the practice of the Canadian Pacific Railway. As I said yesterday, it is proposed to regularize this situation by giving the railway company the corporate powers necessary for that purpose. When I presented the resolution, I said, as reported on page 3198 of Hansard of April 26, 1955:
There is no suggestion either that in granting this power the railway shall be free from the necessity of complying with the requirements of provincial governments so far as provincial laws apply to the operation of motor vehicles owned by the company.
There is no intention on my part of going beyond what was said by me during the resolution stage or yesterday on the second reading, though it may perhaps disappoint some hon. members of this house who I gather would like to see the very broadest powers in the matter of highway transportation vested in the Canadian National Railways. I had thought, and it had been so represented to me, that the powers in the matter of highway transport contained in the bill were subject to considerable restrictions, first of all, in the enumeration of the powers itself, and, second, by the use of the expression "in conjunction with or in substitution for rail services." It was believed, and quite honestly I shared that belief, that this was a restriction of the highway transportation powers which it was proposed to give. But, after listening to what has been said by hon. members during the course of this debate and the representations that have been made to me since the bill has been made public, I have come to the conclusion that the bill itself does go beyond the limits which I had set forth when the resolution was presented. For that reason I should like to supplement what I said yesterday with regard to the amendment which we proposed to meet.
I might perhaps sum up as briefly as I can the amendment that I contemplate in order to meet the limitations which I had in mind, so that the bill will conform entirely with what I said, both in the resolution stage and yesterday. I said first of all yesterday that it was proposed to amend the bill so that the declaration that the railway or other transportation works of the company are works for the general advantage of Canada should not extend to the companies listed in part III of the first schedule to the act. Part III of the first schedule includes of course, as I said specifically yesterday, Canadian National Transportation, Limited. In the same sense, it was never my intention that
[Mr. Marler.l
the declaration contained in the bill to the effect that the transportation works were works for the general advantage of Canada should extend to cover the highway transportation activities of the Canadian National Railways, under the section of the bill by which it is proposed to give them power in this matter.
Finally, because I believe the matter should be abundantly clear, I would also propose that the powers which would be granted to the company should be exercised subject to provincial legislation applicable to persons generally.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that you realize that the effect of the amendments that I contemplate is to give to Canadian National Railways the corporate power to operate motor vehicles in connection with its pickup and delivery services and moreover to exercise similar powers in the case of the abandonment of rail lines where the supplying of bus services or truck services in lieu of rail services is made a condition of the order of abandonment granted by the board of transport commissioners.
In effect that would put the railway company in the position of having the corporate powers to carry out these activities and leave it in the position in which it is at present of requiring it to conform to provincial legislation so far as the carrying on of these operations is concerned.

But nothing has been further from our minds, and we have no intention whatever of doing it.
Mr. Speaker, one final word. The Leader of the Opposition this afternoon spoke about the C.P.R. powers respecting branch lines. I will agree wfth what he said, so far as he went. In other words, he made it perfectly clear that Canadian Pacific Railway was in a general sense subject to the provisions of section 183 of the Railway Act, which requires the approval of the board of transport commissioners where a branch line exceeds six miles. He seemed to have forgotten the fact that that applies, not throughout the whole length of the C.P.R. mileage, but that it has the right under its charter to construct branches off its main line of any length west of Callander, Ontario, without the approval of the board of transport commissioners.
In the legislation which is before the house it is not the intention to grant similar powers to the Canadian National Railways. It is intended, as I have said both at the resolution stage and yesterday, to give it the power to build lines not longer than six miles in length without the necessity of parliamentary approval.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture) moved

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 352, respecting the inspection of meat and meat products entering into international and interprovincial trade.

maintopic: INSPECTION OF PRODUCTS ENTERING INTERNATIONAL AND INTERPROVINCIAL TRADE
speechtext: Does the minister wish to make a statement?

maintopic: INSPECTION OF PRODUCTS ENTERING INTERNATIONAL AND INTERPROVINCIAL TRADE
speechtext:
In rising to move the second reading of Bill No. 352, an act respecting the inspection of meat and meat products entering into international and interprovincial trade, I may say that experience over the years has brought us to the conviction that where we have made provision in acts of this kind to enact measures with regard to interprovincial trade as well as intraprovincial trade, we have run into difficulties whenever these measures have been brought before the court.
We have been advised that at this time amendments should be made in this act for the purpose of removing some of the doubtful sections of it. The main purpose is in order to provide for changes which have taken place. The act as it now stands provides for the regulation of the inspection of canned foods such as fruits and fish. Fish are now being taken care of under an act under the fisheries department and therefore that is not required. It is the intention to bring in a general standards act which I hope to bring forward immediately following this particular bill, in order to take care of the other matters which will be removed.
This bill provides for an act dealing specifically with the health inspection of meat and the sanitary inspection of premises and equipment in plants engaged in interprovincial and export meat shipment. Legislation in that respect has existed since 1907 under the Meat and Canned Foods Act, which act deals also with the grading and inspection of any canned foods including fish. Certain minor amendments were desired in the meat inspection legislation to provide for inspection fees to strengthen the authority of the act with respect to plant sanitation requirements and health supervision of imported meats and meat products.
As the provisions of the present act relating to meat inspection have no relation to the provisions with respect to canned fish, fruit and vegetables, the government consider that the occasion would be appropriate to introduce a bill for a separate act having to do with meat inspection. The bill does

Meat Inspection
not in substance differ materially from the meat inspection provisions of the Meat and Canned Foods Act. It provides that meats or meat products shall move interprovincially or for export only from establishments which meet prescribed conditions with respect to sanitation and in which all meats and meat products have been inspected and passed for health. It provides also that imported meats shall be subject to inspection on a basis similar to that prevailing in Canada. It is proposed that when the required regulations have been made under the new legislation, the corresponding regulations under the Meat and Canned Foods Act can be revoked.
I should like to move second reading of the bill.

maintopic: INSPECTION OF PRODUCTS ENTERING INTERNATIONAL AND INTERPROVINCIAL TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think much discussion is necessary on this bill. As I understand it, it is simply taking out the meat inspection part of the Meat and Canned Foods Act and putting it into a separate bill. That is my understanding of it. Of course, as the minister said, import restrictions for imported meat products are to be taken under this bill now.
This bill has been in use for many years. It is a wonderful thing for the protection of the consuming public in that all plants having to do with interprovincial or international trade must be inspected by inspectors of the health of animals division. Confidence in a product makes for higher consumption of the product and naturally, in many cases, increases the price to the producer of those various products.
As to many small plants across the country which are not now under inspection, there is some justification for believing that it might be a good idea if, in co-operation with the provincial and municipal officials, there could be some way of utilizing the services of existing veterinary inspectors in various localities across the country in order to see that these other small abattoirs and killer stations come under some kind of inspection similar to that provided in this bill. They are, of course, under inspection now by municipal authorities. But I regret to say that there are some cases in which that inspection is not satisfactory. Some cases have been known where meat has been sold over the counter when it was not fit for human consumption.
I think something could be worked out. I think there has been good co-operation between most of the provincial governments and the federal authorities along that line. By working through the provincial governments and the municipal authorities I think something could be worked out along that line. I wonder whether the government has ever 
given consideration to that matter or whether they would give consideration to something along that line.

maintopic: INSPECTION OF PRODUCTS ENTERING INTERNATIONAL AND INTERPROVINCIAL TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in supporting this bill may I say that I think perhaps the matter of meat inspection is something that needs to be made uniform. The question that occurred to me is whether or not the present standards have been found to be sufficiently comprehensive to cover the situations arising in different parts of Canada. I believe it is the intention of the minister to introduce another bill called the standards act under which the standards will be established so that the inspection set up under this bill can be directed by standards which will be uniform throughout the whole of Canada. In the general trend of business today, with Canada taking her place as the leading food manufacturer, I think this kind of legislation is a necessary and a good thing.
I should like to have from the minister a statement as to whether he expects that this legislation will result in a large increase in inspection staff over what he already has under the present act, namely the Meat and Canned Foods Act. What steps have been taken to co-operate with the various provinces with a view to getting the inspection uniform? There is provincial inspection of small abattoirs. I understand this has to do largely with canned goods. But the matter of inspection and of having uniformity will be a good thing for Canada. On those two points I think we can support the principle of the bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext:
that the house go into committee on the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish national standards for agricultural products and to regulate international and interprovincial trade in agricultural products and to provide that the governor in council may make regulations for the licensing of dealers to deal in any agricultural products shipped from or to a place outside the province in which such dealer carries on business, and for the issue, cancellation and suspension of such licences, including the prescribing of fees for the issue thereof.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the present time there are five statutes prescribing national standards and grading requirements for various agricultural products. These statutes are the Canada Dairy Products Act, 1952; Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act, 1952; Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act, 1952; Meat and Canned Foods Act, 1952; and the Maple Products Industry Act, 1952.

Agricultural Products
The purpose of the new act is to provide acceptable, uniform authorities for establishing grade standards and to perform the grading and inspection for all agricultural products previously covered by five separate acts administered by the Department of Agriculture.
The new general act is patterned after the Canada Dairy Products Act enacted in 1951 which has proven satisfactory for dairy products. It provides authority for establishing substantially the same regulations as now exist but is considered to have the purposes and intentions more clearly defined and restricted to the established and accepted field of federal jurisdiction specifically related to grade and quality standards for agricultural products.
The act will provide as in the past for the actual grading of certain products by federal graders, and for others, the application of the established grades and standards by the trade with subsequent checking of the applied standards by federal inspectors and detention until they are made to comply with the official standards when found necessary.
The provisions of the act will apply where the products enter into interprovincial or export trade, or where, as a result of legislation on the part of a province or the voluntary action on the part of an individual, the product bears a grade name established pursuant to this act. Compulsory grading of a product moving intraprovincially will therefore depend upon action by the provinces.
In addition to defining standards and carrying out the grading and inspection operations, the act provides as in the past for regulatory services with respect to such matters as packaging, marking and shipping of products, operation of grading establishment and dealing in products exported from or imported into a province.
It will be noted by the hon. member for Selkirk that what he was talking about is really provided for in this legislation.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister has given us a good explanation of what is to come in the bill which is to cover the legislation now to be found in five different acts. I do not think there is need for any general discussion until we have the bill and see what it actually contains. However, there are a few remarks I should like to make at this time.
I am not saying that it is not a good idea to have farm products graded, but the fact is that while everything a farmer sells is sold under grade not many of the articles he buys

are sold in that way. There are many consumer products sold across this country which are not graded in any way. They are supposed to be marked, but the contents may not be fully graded. For instance, you cannot tell by looking at a shoe whether or not the sole is all leather.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: Or cardboard.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: You have to try to grade such an article yourself at the time you purchase it. I think it would be good business on the part of this government to see that other products are sold to the consumer under grade.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was very much interested in the comments made by the hon. member who has resumed his seat. He may not be aware of the fact but he is advocating some social planning. He does not want to interfere with free enterprise, but under free enterprise we have some inferior products being marketed. I am all for that, but that really is not why I rose to speak.
About 20 years ago we had quite an extensive inquiry into price spreads and at that time it was found that consumers were at the mercy of many of the canning and processing companies. I had hoped that before now we would have a more uniform standard in Canada so that if you bought a can of vegetables marked "choice" you could expect a choice product. However, we do not seem to have made very much progress in getting uniform standards to apply to all preserving or canning companies in Canada.
When the people where I live sell their wheat it is subject to very rigid standards. Those who sell pork products must sell according to grade. As the hon. member for Selkirk has pointed out on a number of occasions, when a hog is one point lower than a certain standard the farmer must pay a heavy penalty. It is not unreasonable to ask that those engaged in canning or processing should observe certain standards.
Those of us who come from the west are in the habit of buying apples which are carefully packed and labelled. When you buy a fancy grade you know that when you open the box you will find exactly what you expect. But when we come to Ontario we find that unless we buy British Columbia apples we invariably get some inferior apples regardless of the price we pay. It seems to me that, if the farmers in one section of Canada are expected to produce a product according to fixed standards, the Minister of Agriculture should be able to report more progress than he has in seeing to it that in all parts of

Canada those who produce agricultural products would be encouraged to produce a uniform product, and those who are engaged in canning sell choice quality products in cans that are labelled "choice quality". In standard or choice canned goods, whether canned in the east, in the west or in the central part of Canada, there should be goods of similar qualities. At some time before the bill is passed I should like the minister to indicate what progress is being made in seeing that products which enter into international and interprovincial trade should measure up to standards which are applicable to all parts of Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think that the resolution will require long discussion. Certainly when the bill is brought up for second reading we shall have much fuller discussion on it, but it seems to me that this would be a good chance to ask the minister if his proposed bill does provide some protection for livestock dealers in Ontario who have for years past been victimized by dealers in this way, that these dealers will pay a certain rate for feed grain and when the feed is delivered they find it has been adulterated and they have got an inferior quality. Quite a number of complaints have been registered in this house against that sort of thing, and unfortunately the blame is placed on the western farmer rather than on the unscrupulous dealer who is doing that sort of adulteration. I believe that a good deal of that is being done, not only in Ontario but also in British Columbia.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: It is not the farmer's fault.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: It is not the farmer's fault at all; that is well known. But I am wondering if the measure which is contemplated by this resolution does make provision for regulating that sort of thing.

speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, grain marketing is not under my department; it is under the Department of Trade and Commerce. The wheat board, which handles this product, operates under the Department of Trade and Commerce, and so does the board of grain commissioners, and all the grading of grain and everything associated with that is under the board of grain commissioners and does not come under this bill. This bill deals with dairy products, fruit, vegetables, honey, livestock and livestock products, maple products, meat and canned foods. Those are covered by the five acts which are now being brought under this one.
Agricultural Products

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: I listened very carefully when the minister read his list of matters which the act is supposed to cover, and I did not hear him mention grain and feed grains. That is the reason why I asked the question. It seems to me that, though the wheat board has control of the marketing of grains and though the wheat board comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce, it would be possible to have a measure brought in by my hon. friend's own department that would cover the licensing of dealers as he contemplates licensing dealers in other products, so that inspection and checking could be carried out perhaps through powers delegated to his inspectors from the Department of Trade and Commerce.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: Unfortunately the condition is exactly the same in connection with the grain as it is in connection with the apples. My hon. friend from Mackenzie was speaking about buying apples in Ontario and buying them in Saskatchewan. We do not grow apples for sale in Saskatchewan. They grow a few in his part of the country, but very few apples are grown for sale in Saskatchewan. About the only person who grows them for sale, that I know of, is the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, who does not happen to be here tonight. So we buy our apples from outside the province, and all the apples we get are more or less under the control of the federal authority. The grading and inspection and that kind of thing are more or less taken care of. For example, here in the province of Ontario, I drive to Toronto and on the way back I see a stand at the side of the road and I stop to buy a pound of apples. I look at them to see if the grade suits me. But there is nothing we can do in this parliament to regulate that kind of trade. That is intraprovincial trade. When we try to regulate that by means of an act, the act, when it goes to court, is declared ultra vires. One of the reasons why we are putting through this legislation at the present time is to take out of the act some of those provisions that are in now which, if it ever came to court, would result in one or other of the five acts here proposed being thrown out and declared ultra vires.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: With regard to canned vegetables produced in Ontario and sold all over Canada, is it not possible to enforce the regulations so that they would be up to standard?

speechtext:

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE

speechtext: Since the hon. member for Peace River has brought up the matter of grain going into Ontario, perhaps if the minister would look up his regulations he may find that they now have jurisdiction over mixed feeds. subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: I am neither a lawyer nor a constitutional lawyer, but we have been dealing with this thing now for 20 years. My understanding is that when grain is shipped from the west to, let us say, Goderich or any other point in eastern Canada, it is shipped there and delivered to the individual who bought it. Through the grading of grain in the west we can control what it is that is delivered to the person at any particular point. But after it gets to that point and is being delivered outside of there, whatever action is provided for is provided for provincially. If we attempt to deal with it we get into trouble.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: In view of what the hon. member for Mackenzie has just said with regard to the quality of British Columbia apples, I wonder how he can claim such high regard for B.C. apples that were recently found to be so inferior in Scotland. I believe that commodities grown and canned in southern Ontario are without peer. They will claim the attention of particular purchasers.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: I have listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Mackenzie. I realize immediately that when he buys canned goods he does not even look at the label. There are three grades of canned vegetables, namely standard, choice and fancy, which is the best grade. Not only are these canned goods all inspected and graded but most of the products that go into the cans are graded before canning. Today in Ontario, under the Ontario marketing act, these products are graded when they go to the factory. I hear some of my hon. friends over to my left laughing.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: It is empty laughter.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext: There is a staff of inspectors in Ontario and in the rest of Canada working under the Department of Agriculture. These inspectors go to these factories and inspect these goods frequently. But the point is this, and I come back to it again. There are three grades. If you buy the standard grade, you get the poorest quality. But if you want a real good grade, you buy the fancy grade. That is why there is such a great difference in the quality of the product. If you are going to buy canned goods, always look at the label and know exactly what you are buying.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL STANDARDS AND REGULATE TRADE
speechtext:
I do not intend to enter into any discussion as to the relative merits of grades of agricultural products in Ontario as compared with agricultural products in any other province. I think this resolution now before us could be extremely important if the legislation introduced in fact carries out the suggestions made in this resolution. The resolution reads as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish national standards for agricultural products and to regulate international and interprovincial trade in agricultural products and to provide that the governor in council may make regulations for the licensing of dealers to deal in any agricultural products shipped from or to a place outside the province in which such dealer carries on business, and for the issue, cancellation and suspension of such licences, including the prescribing of fees for the issue thereof.
I suggest that this resolution is sufficiently broad in scope that it should contain all of those resolutions and all of the powers that have been suggested from time to time by the farm organizations of this country when they have asked the government to establish legislation that would be governed by a board of livestock commissioners.
Some reference has been made to the Canada Grain Act and to the board of grain commissioners. Faulty and inadequate as that legislation may be, nevertheless it is vastly superior to any legislation we have had to date in Canada dealing with interprovincial and export trade in other agricultural products. While it is true that a feeder in Ontario may not be definitely certain as to the quality of the feed product when he buys it from a commercial organization, nevertheless if that farmer is able to purchase directly from the wheat board a quantity of grain which has been graded according to the standards of the Canada Grain Act and which has the stamp of approval of the board of grain commissioners, that feeder is assured of getting a quality product.
The trouble is not with the regulations under the Canada Grain Act. The difficulty is mainly not in the standards established under the Canada Grain Act. The difficulty is that so far the government has failed to adopt legislation that, with respect to feed that he purchases from a dealer, will guarantee to the eastern feeder the same standards as those that are provided for in the Canada Grain Act. I should like to see the government establish a board of livestock commissioners that will have the power to do all of the things mentioned in this resolution and additional things. I should like to see the standards that are set up for livestock and other agricultural products taken right back to the producer so that when the producer delivers a carload of beef to a packing
Agricultural Products
company he is certain to obtain for that beef the grade and the price for that grade that may be finally approved by such a board of livestock commissioners.
In the legislation that is adopted I think it is important not only to see to it that proper standards are set up but to see that the benefits from those standards shall accrue to the producer. I should like to see this legislation carried even another step forward. I should like to see a national livestock marketing board or some type of national livestock selling agency so that the producers themselves may have some control over the buying and selling of their products. Certainly the resolution we have before us this evening is the type of resolution that would be of great benefit to the producers if properly enforced.
I am glad that the government at this time is consolidating acts so that the public may know what power the government has and what legislation it is actually using. When the minister is considering consolidation of acts, he might look at his act which is entitled "An act for the support of the prices of agricultural products during the transition from war to peace"; another act entitled "The Agricultural Products Board Act"; and a further act entitled "An act to provide for the marketing of agricultural products in interprovincial and export trade". That is a series of acts that certainly in many ways duplicate and overlap and it is a series of acts which, I may say incidentally, are little used. I therefore think it is a step in the right direction that the legislation is being consolidated. I should like to see the government go one step further and establish a board of livestock commissioners such as that suggested by the hon. member for Yorkton in his resolution under "Notices of Motions", to be found at page 15 of today's order paper and which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into early consideration the advisability of appointing a board of livestock commissioners in Canada for the purpose of regulating and controlling the assembling, grading, transporting, marketing and exporting of livestock and livestock products, and that such board should include adequate representation appointed on the recommendation of the producers' organizations.
If the resolution before us tonight were expanded to include the proposition advanced by the hon. member for Yorkton I think we would have legislation that would not only be more effective but legislation that has been requested by our many farm organizations.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.

subtopic: MEASURE TO REPEAL EXISTING LEGISLATION AND SUBSTITUTE NEW ACT

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: MEASURE TO REPEAL EXISTING LEGISLATION AND SUBSTITUTE NEW ACT
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to repeal the Yukon Quartz Mining Act, chapter 301 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, and to make provision by means of a new act for all substantive rights relating to quartz mining in the Yukon, including the rights to stake and acquire mineral claims and leases, and to provide for certain modifications in the administration of the law.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: MEASURE TO REPEAL EXISTING LEGISLATION AND SUBSTITUTE NEW ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the legislation to which this resolution relates is of an unusual character in parliament. Legislation on mining is normally provincial and a matter of provincial jurisdiction, but so far as the territories are concerned most matters of a provincial character are handled by the respective commissioners and councils. There is an exception though in the case of matters relating to natural resources. The natural resources of the Yukon and Northwest Territories are held by the federal government in the same way as the resources of the western provinces were held by the federal government before 1930. The resources of the soil and subsoil in the territories were originally governed by regulations established under the Dominion Lands Act which was passed in 1872 and which was replaced by the Territorial Lands Act in 1950.
There are two exceptions to the general coverage of the Territorial Lands Act. They are the Yukon Placer Mining Act which governs placer mining in the Yukon, and the Yukon Quartz Mining Act which covers quartz mining in the Yukon. The Yukon Placer Mining Act was passed in 1906. It was the governing act for placer gold development in the Yukon following the Klondike rush ten years earlier, and it still governs placer mining for gold near Dawson and elsewhere. There is no intention to modify the Yukon Placer Mining Act at this time.


The Yukon Quartz Mining Act was passed in 1924. Prior to that time quartz mining was governed by regulations under the Dominion Lands Act, as all mining in the Northwest Territories is now governed by regulations under the Territorial Lands Act. The act of 1924 simply put in statutory form the regulations in force at that time. It provides no authority to make general regulations and there has not been any overall revision in the 31 years since it was passed.
But conditions have changed considerably since 1924. The development of the Yukon is proceeding at a steadily increasing pace. Conditions of mining and prospecting have changed, and there is no doubt that the act has become out of date in respect of many of its provisions which are of importance to mining in the Yukon. Some of the clauses in the present act are not capable of proper interpretation. Some others do not take into account many improvements that have been devised in recent years in the field of mining legislation, and some others are not as favourable to mining development as more advanced clauses existing in the legislation of several of the provinces.
In the intervening years since 1924 we have been shown a great many defects in the provisions and operation of the act. Revision is required, I submit, if unsatisfactory and out of date provisions are not to have a deteriorating effect on the development of the Yukon. The legislation contemplated by the resolution before the house is to achieve that revision. The original intention two years ago was to repeal the Yukon Quartz Mining Act entirely and to have quartz mining in the Yukon placed under the Territorial Lands Act, the same as mining in the Northwest Territories. It would have meant almost no statutory provisions and everything would have been covered by regulations of the governor in council.
A bill to achieve that purpose was placed on the order paper at the session of 1953-54, but it became clear then that there was considerable opposition in the Yukon to this course, and of course the hon. member for the Yukon did voice that opposition very strongly. The opposition was mainly to the abolition of statutory provisions. It seemed that most of the prospectors in the Yukon did not wish to have the entire regime, including substantive rights, subject to control by regulation. Because of that opposition and differences of opinion it was decided that the best course would be to have an impartial and expert examination of the situation by a qualified man with wide experience in mining in Canada. I took the

advice of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I discussed the matter with various interested persons, including the hon. member for the Yukon, and I asked Mr. George Edward Cole if he would serve as commissioner. Mr. Cole has been in the mining industry in Canada for 53 years. He worked in the British Columbia, Ontario and Manitoba mining fields. He had overseas service from 1915 to 1919. In 1928 he was appointed chief inspector of mines for Manitoba and in 1930 was appointed director of mines for that province. He retired from that position in 1945. From 1941 to 1945 he was president of the association of professional engineers of Manitoba. He is a past president of the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy.
Mr. Cole interviewed most of the people in the Yukon who are interested in mining, as well as the mining people elsewhere in Canada. He spent some weeks in the Yukon and looked thoroughly into the whole situation. As I say, he discussed it with a number of people, including the hon. member for the Yukon, who has always shown a special interest in mining in his territory. Then, he submitted his report to me on June 18, 1954. I believe it is a very good report and has clarified the position considerably. When I was in the Yukon last summer I discussed the report personally with many of the mining and prospecting interests there. After these discussions, after studying the mining laws of the various provinces, and after thoroughly studying the report, I became convinced that Mr. Cole's recommendations were basically sound. The Cole report has, therefore, formed the basis of the new legislation to be introduced by this resolution.
Now, Mr. Chairman, since the Cole report forms the basis of the legislation I feel that the best course to follow would be to outline the recommendations which the report contains. I believe, however, this would be a good point to move the adjournment of the debate before I deal with the various points made.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We shall continue tomorrow with the business that I indicated on Friday night.

When the minister announced the business of the house on Friday last, I asked him about the government notice of motion on the order paper providing for the establishment of a committee on atomic energy and research. At that time he replied he was not in a position to say when it would
Business of the House be put on for debate, but he would try to answer on Monday. The minister said nothing about it last night nor tonight.
I point out to him that on February 3 of this year the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Macleod, as found at page 795 of Hansard, stated:
-it is the intention of the government to propose a committee to study atomic energy as well as research generally.
Then, on March 29, the government placed on the order paper a motion to set up this committee. That is almost two months ago, yet we have no word as to when the government proposes to proceed with the setting up of this committee. I point out to the minister that he is hoping to get this house prorogued by the end of next month. I believe the time has come when the government should take steps to set up this committee, and I would ask the minister when it is proposed to move the motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
All that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has stated, Mr. Speaker, is quite correct. I feel I should point out, however, that what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said on February 3 was that we would propose a committee. Consultations were had after that with interested persons and the personnel obtained. Then, on March 29, a motion was put on the order paper. I believe everyone recalls that the minister concerned left for Australia within five or six days thereafter and only returned on May 5.
Since that time I have not found it possible to call this item, having in mind the fact that we have legislation on the order paper and we are still attempting to get legislation into the hands of the committee. I gave consideration to this a week ago, and at that time it did seem to me that if we hoped to bring the session to a close reasonably soon it would be necessary for the committees to complete their work rather than adding to their work. For that reason it seemed to me that, unless there was an urgent need for this committee at this session, it would be desirable not to call it. Now, this particular committee is not one that can be dealt with in one, two, three or four meetings or even in as many weeks. In the past there has been serious and leisurely consideration of these very important matters. On past occasions the committee has travelled outside of Ottawa, and I would expect it would if it were set up now.
Under the circumstances, I do feel it would not be desirable to proceed with this motion, unless as I have said there are reasons I have

Business of the House not been informed about why we should proceed with it at the present time. However, if hon. members feel there are reasons I would be glad to hear them and consider the matter further later this week.

During the session last year we were given to understand that a committee on atomic energy would be set up this year. This is a field in which there have been rapid developments in the last year. We now have intimations from members of the government that atomic energy is to be used for peacetime purposes and that private industry has been invited to participate. I think the minister is quite wrong when he intimates there is no hurry about this question. I suggest that this is one of the questions about which parliament should be informed. The purpose of having such a committee was to help keep members in touch with this development.
I urge upon him that the government proceed without any further delay to get the committee set up and at least get the work started. I think we could finish the work on atomic energy before the end of this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As I have said, I will consider all the representations that are made. I am informed that what my hon. friend says in the latter part of his remarks is not so, and it would not be likely that the atomic energy portion of the work of the committee could be completed in any reasonable time. However, I shall be glad to consider it and discuss it with him and any other members who may be interested.

speechtext: With regard to the business for tomorrow, do we go on with Friday night's list from the point we had reached or do we pick up any of the items that have been moved up a stage or two in the meantime? I think it may be more satisfactory if the minister would tell us, one, two, three, what he has in mind for tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not know what my hon. friend has in mind. I have not been in the house for the last hour and a half.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We have been making good progress in your absence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Fine; I shall stay out from now on. I understand that we are dealing with the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. Then, we have the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the Blind Persons Act. Thursday and Friday we will take post office and agriculture.

speechtext: My question related to the matter of third reading of Bill No. 352 and second reading of the other bill in the name of the Minister of Agriculture. Those are the things we did while the minister was out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What does my hon. friend want to take up tomorrow?
